newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech c.bank calls for 1998 budget surplus.
newsitem.headline: Czech c.bank calls for 1998 budget surplus.

text.p: The Czech National Bank (CNB) would prefer that the 1998 state budget show a surplus equal to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP), CNB vice governor Pavel Kysilka told journalists.

"It would be very useful for this year to have a balanced budget, moreover the economy would benefit from a relatively high surplus next year. It would be very important to have the state budget in a surplus of about three percent of GDP," he said after a closed-door conference of business leaders.

The Czech government, soon after the central bank was forced to float the crown on May 27 amid speculative attacks on the currency, adopted its second austerity package in as many months aimed at slowing domestic demand.
A current account deficit at over eight percent of GDP brought on by a huge demand for imports, was one of the key factors which led speculators to make a move on the currency.
The government plan called for spending cuts leading to a balancing of the budget this year, and a surplus budget in 1998, but politicians have been arguing over how to achieve this.
Finance Minister Ivan Pilip said earlier this month that he expects to build the 1998 budget with a 10 billion crown surplus.
Czech gross domestic product, in nominal terms, totalled 1.490 trillion crowns in 1996, with forecasts this year of 10.5 to 12.5 percent nominal growth.
Kysilka said that May's 11.7 percent year-on-year nominal industrial wage growth "is still too high for the economy."
"But I also understand that it is almosst impossible at this point to press the figure lower," he said, adding that he would like to see nominal wage growth below inflation next year.
"The economy would need lower growth in domestic demand than GDP growth. "I realise this may be difficult to achieve in the near future, but this is our aim," he said.
